turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah, that's right. And again, here, this is a great example. So again, the task level of, like, "Design the perfect icon," is going to be, all right, the AI's going to do that all day long. If it gives you a thousand icon designs, it's going to be great. It's going to be fantastic, whatever. And by the way, there will still be some level of human icon design or whatever, but AI is going to get really good at that. But what are we trying to do, kind of capital D design of, like, "All right, what is this thing for, and how is this going to function in a world of human beings? And is this going to make people happy when they use it? Is this going to make people feel good about themselves? Is it going to fit into the rest of their life? Is it going to, I don't know, challenge them in the right way?" All of these kinds of higher level questions that the great designers have always thought about. (00:52:40): The job of designer will involve much more of those higher level, more important components, and then again, with AI doing a lot more of the underlying tasks. And so one way to think about it is, I don't know, you think of the world's best designers, Jony Ive or whatever, and you could be like, "Wow." Like, if I'm a designer today, if I'm a 25-year-old designer and I aspire to be Jony Ive in a decade, it's all of a sudden, I have a new path that I can use to get there, which is... Because Jony did everything. He did it without AI. Now, a young designer tends to be like, "Wow, if I really harness AI in a decade, I'm going to be like the best designer of the world's ever seen because it's not just going to be me. It's going to be me, plus being so super empowered by this technology to be able to do so much more. And then so much more of my time and attention is going to be able to be focused on these higher-level things that most designers never get to." (00:53:29): I think that's going to be another great example of that.
turns.zh:
是的，没错。再说一次，这里就是一个很好的例子。所以，任务层面，比如“设计一个完美的图标”，人工智能会全天候地处理这个任务。如果它给你一千个图标设计方案，那当然很棒。无论如何，这都会很出色。不过，还是会有一定程度的人工图标设计工作存在，但人工智能在这方面会变得非常擅长。但我们真正要做的，是那种大写的D级设计，比如，“这个产品是用来做什么的？它在人类世界中如何运作？使用它的人会感到快乐吗？它能让人们对自己感觉良好吗？它能融入他们的生活吗？它能以正确的方式挑战他们吗？”这些都是伟大的设计师一直思考的高级问题。

（00:52:40）：设计师的工作将更多地涉及这些高级、更重要的部分，而人工智能则会承担更多基础任务。所以，可以这样想：你想到世界上最伟大的设计师，比如乔尼·艾夫（Jony Ive）之类的，你可能会惊叹道。比如，如果我今天是一名25岁的设计师，十年后想成为乔尼·艾夫那样的人物，突然间，我有了一条新的成功之路，那就是……因为乔尼什么都做了。他在没有人工智能的情况下做到了。而现在，年轻设计师往往会想：“哇，如果十年后我能充分利用人工智能，我将成为世界上最出色的设计师，因为这不再只是我一个人的功劳。这将是我自己的能力，再加上这项技术带来的巨大助力，能让我做得更多。然后，我就能把更多时间和精力投入到大多数设计师从未接触过的高级事务中。”

（00:53:29）：我认为这将是另一个很好的例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So maybe what I'm hearing here is kind of this T-shaped strategy of if you want to be successful in any three of these roles, be very, very, very good at that specific role: product management, engineering design. And then get good enough at these other two roles.
turns.zh: 所以，也许我在这里听到的是一种T型策略：如果你想在上述三个角色中任意一个取得成功，就必须在那个特定角色上非常、非常、非常出色：产品管理、工程设计。然后在其他两个角色上也要足够出色。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: I think that's great. I think that's really relevant. And then Scott Adamson, firstly, just passed away, which is a real tragedy. But I referred for years to, actually, Scott Adams. He had this famous career advice he would give people, which I think makes a lot of sense. Which dovetails with what you're saying, which-
turns.zh: 我认为这很棒。我认为这真的很有意义。然后斯科特·亚当森（Scott Adamson）首先刚刚去世了，这真是个悲剧。但多年来，我一直提及斯科特·亚当斯（Scott Adams）。他曾给人们提供过著名的职业建议，我认为这很有道理。这与你所说的很契合——

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: ... advice he would give people which I think makes a lot of sense, which dovetails with what you're saying, which is he used to say it's like, look, he said, "I could have been a pretty good cartoonist or I could have been pretty good at business, but the fact that I was a cartoonist who understood business made me spectacularly great at making Dilbert." Because even the world's best cartoonist who didn't understand business could have never written Dilbert, and then the world's best business people who didn't know how to do cartoons couldn't have done Dilbert. It took somebody who actually had both of those skills to be able to make Dilbert which is one of the most successful cartoons in history. (00:54:32): And so the way Scott always described it was that from a career development standpoint, the additive effect of being good at two things is more than double. The additive effect of being good at three things is more than triple because you become a super relevant specialist in the combination of the domains, and, look, I mean, you see this all over the economy. I mean, you see this all over the economy, but I'll give you an example. Hollywood, just Hollywood as an example. There are a lot of writers who can't direct a movie and they can be very successful writers. There are a lot of directors who can't write a movie. They can be very successful directors. But the superstars in the entertainment industry are the people who can write and direct. They don't have a term for those. They call us auteurors, and those are the people who are the real creative forces that move the field. (00:55:20): And so again, and by the way, Hollywood, actually it's really funny, I've been spending a lot of time talking to Hollywood people about AI. Hollywood has the same Mexican stand-off going right now that we describe in tech, except in Hollywood, for example, for filmmaking, it's the director, it's the writer, and the actor. Because the director is now thinking, "Wow, I don't need the writer anymore because the AI can write the script and I don't need the actor anymore because I can have AI actors." The writer is saying, "Well, I don't need the director because I can direct the movie and the AI can do the actors." And the actor is saying, "I don't need either one of these guys. I can have the AI direct the thing, I can have the AI write the thing and I'm just going to show up and do my performance." (00:55:53): And so it's the same kind of triangular configuration, and again, what's great about it is they're all correct. Each person in each of those three fields is going to be able to expand laterally and pick up those additional skills, and then as a consequence, you're going to have more people who can write and direct or write and act or direct and act or do all three. (00:56:13): I think to your point, your T-shaped thing, I think that's going to be true basically across the entire economy. And if you think about the T, if you think about the T configuration, it's like, yeah, the breadth, the top of the T is like how many individual domains are you familiar enough with to be able to use the AI tools to be able to do really good work. And then this part of the T is how deep can you go in at least one of those domains so that you really, really deeply know what you're doing. But if you're super deep on coding and you can use AI to do design and you can use AI to do product management, that's your T right there, and you're a triple threat at the top of the T, but with this level of technical grounding underneath that. (00:56:50): I mean, at that point, again, you're the super-powered individual, you're going to be able to just perform like sheets of magic, for example, in terms of designing and building your products that people in my generation couldn't have even dreamed of. And so I think that this is a universal kind of theory that I think can apply across the entire economy.
turns.zh:
接下来是斯科特（Scott）给出的建议，我认为这非常有道理，也与你所说的观点不谋而合。他曾说过：“我本可以成为一名相当不错的漫画家，或者在商业领域表现出色，但正是因为我既是漫画家又懂商业，才让我能出色地创作出《呆伯特》（Dilbert）。”因为即便是最优秀的漫画家如果不了解商业，也永远无法创作出《呆伯特》；而最优秀的商人如果不懂漫画，也无法创作出《呆伯特》。只有同时具备这两项技能的人，才能创作出《呆伯特》这款史上最成功的漫画。（00:54:32）：从职业发展角度看，擅长两项技能的叠加效应是双倍的，擅长三项技能的叠加效应更是三倍有余，因为你能在多个领域的交叉点上成为超级专家。看看整个经济领域，你随处可见这种现象。我以好莱坞为例。许多编剧无法执导电影，但他们可以成为非常成功的编剧；许多导演无法编剧，但他们可以成为非常成功的导演。但娱乐界的超级巨星是既能编剧又能执导的人。业界对这类人才没有特定称呼，我们称他们为“作者”，而这些人正是推动行业创新的真正力量。（00:55:20）：再说回好莱坞，有趣的是，我最近花了很多时间与好莱坞人士探讨人工智能问题。好莱坞目前正面临着与科技领域相同的僵局，只不过在好莱坞，僵局发生在导演、编剧和演员之间。比如导演现在认为：“哇，我不再需要编剧了，因为人工智能能写剧本；我也不需要演员了，因为我可以用人工智能演员。”编剧则说：“好吧，我不需要导演了，因为我能自己执导电影，而人工智能能处理演员部分。”演员则说：“我不需要他们中的任何一个。我可以让人工智能执导，让人工智能写剧本，然后我只需来展示我的表演。”（00:55:53）：这就是同样的三角结构。重要的是，每个领域的人都能横向扩展，掌握额外的技能。因此，将来会有更多人能同时编剧和执导、编剧和表演、执导和表演。（00:56:13）：我认为你提到的T型人才，基本上适用于整个经济领域。如果你思考T型结构，会发现：T的宽度（顶部）是，你对多少个领域足够熟悉，从而能利用人工智能工具做出出色的工作；T的深度（底部）是，你在至少一个领域能深入到何种程度，从而真正精通该领域。但如果你在编程方面非常精通，能用人工智能做设计、做产品管理，这就是你的T型结构，你是T型结构顶端的三面手，但同时又有扎实的技术基础。（00:56:50）：我的意思是，在这个
再次强调，你是拥有超强能力的人，你将能够轻松实现各种神奇的成果。比如，在设计和制造产品方面，就能创造出令我们这代人连做梦都想不到的成果。因此，我认为这是一项普适的理论，适用于整个经济领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to invent a new framework right now. Okay, forget the T framework. I'm picturing an F sideways or an E where there's three, two or three, I don't know, downward parts. And so what I'm hearing is get good at least two or three.
turns.zh: 我现在要发明一个新的框架。好吧，不提T框架了。我想象的是一个侧放的F，或者一个E，有三个、两个或三个，我也不知道，向下的部分。那么我的理解是，至少要精通两到三项技能。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's right. I think that's right. Yeah, the combination, yeah. My friend, Larry Summers, had a different version of the Scott Adams thing, which is he used to tell people, he said, " The key for career planning is," he said, "don't be fungible." He's an economist and so that was economic speaking. What that means essentially is don't be replaceable. And so don't be a cog, and what that meant was don't just be one thing. So if you're, quote unquote, again, just a designer, just a product manager, just a coder, then in theory you can be swapped in or out. (00:57:52): But if you have this E or F laying on the side kind of thing, and if you have this combination of things that's actually quite rare, then all of a sudden you're not fungible. Not only you're not fungible, you're actually massively important because you're one of the only people in the world who can actually do that combination of things. And yeah, your ability to not become one of those people is just titanically enhanced with AI as compared to anything we've ever seen before.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得没错。我觉得没错。是的，这种组合，对。我的朋友拉里·萨默斯对斯科特·亚当斯的观点有不同的理解。他过去常对人说：“职业规划的关键是，”他说：“别成为可替代的。”他是经济学家，所以这是在用经济学的术语说话。意思基本上就是别可替代。别当个齿轮，也就是别只会一件事。所以如果你只是个设计师、产品经理、程序员，那理论上你可以被随意替换。（00:57:52）但如果你有这种侧放的E或者F，或者有这种非常罕见的技能组合，那突然间你就不可替代了。你不仅不可替代，你实际上还非常重要，因为你是世界上唯一能做这种技能组合的人之一。而随着AI的出现，你不成为这样的人的能力得到了极大的提升，相比我们之前见过的任何技术都要强得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so interesting because I've worked with people that are good at these two skills and they were always called unicorns at the company. She can code and design, oh my god. And what I'm hearing here is this is what you need to become. You need to become really good at at least two things there. I think you used the term smoke stack or something where it's like PM over here, engineer design, and what I'm hearing here is you need to get good at at least two of these skills. The silos of these two roles are disappearing.
turns.zh: 这太有趣了，因为我曾和精通这两项技能的人共事过，他们在公司里总是被称为"独角兽"。她既能编程又能设计，天哪。而我在这里听到的是，这就是你需要成为的人。你需要精通至少两项技能。我想你用过"烟囱式技能"这个术语，比如产品经理这边，工程师设计那边，而我在这里听到的是，你需要精通其中至少两项技能。这两个角色的壁垒正在消失。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: That's right. That's right. And again, I can't overstress the following, for anybody listening to this, the thing about AI that I think people are just not getting enough benefit out of yet is just it will teach you. This is amazing. There's never been a technology before where you could ask it, "Teach me how to do this thing." And so I always feel like it's like people spend too much... it's one of these things where it's like so much focus on figuring out how to use a large language model is like, "Okay, what am I going to try to get it to do for me?" which is of course very important. But the other side of it is, what can I get it to teach me how to do, and it's just as good at that. And so again, this is this level of latent superpower. (00:59:19): People who really want to improve themselves and develop their career should be spending every spare hour in my view at this point talking on AI, being like, "All right, train me up. Super empower me. Train me, train me how to be... I'm a coder. Train me how to be a product manager." It will happily do that. It knows exactly how to do that. Run me, make me problems... yeah, make me assignments, then evaluate my results. It will do that just as happily as it will do work, quote unquote, for you.
turns.zh: 没错。没错。再说一次，我再怎么强调都不为过，对任何听这个的人来说，AI最让人受益的地方还在于它会教你。这太神奇了。以前从没有一种技术，你可以问它："教我怎么做这件事。"所以我总觉得人们花了太多精力... 人们太专注于如何使用大型语言模型了，比如“好吧，我要让它为我做什么？”这当然很重要。但另一方面，你能让它教你怎么做，它在这方面也同样出色。所以再说一次，这是潜在的超能力级别。（00:59:19）真正想提升自己、发展事业的人，在我看来，现在应该利用每一分钟空闲时间研究AI，说：“好吧，训练我。超级赋能我。训练我，训练我怎么成为... 我是个程序员。训练我怎么成为产品经理。”它会很乐意这么做。它完全知道怎么做。给我出题... 是的，给我布置任务，然后评估我的结果。它会像乐意为你工作一样乐意做这些事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Two tricks I've heard along those lines. One is to watch the output, what the agent is doing and thinking as it's doing the work. So if you're not an engineer, just sit there and watch it think and make decisions, and it's almost become this layer on top of learning to code is learning to see what the agent is doing and thinking because that teaches you about architecture. And the other is, a couple podcast guests have mentioned this, when you get stuck and then you figure out how to unstuck yourself, you ask it, "What could I have done differently? What could I have said that would've avoided this error in the first place?"
turns.zh: 以下是我听过的两个相关技巧。第一个是观察输出，观察智能体在执行任务时的行为和思考过程。即便你不是工程师，只要静静地坐着观察它的思考和决策过程，这几乎就相当于在学习编程之外的另一种学习——学会观察智能体的行为和思维过程，因为这能帮助你理解架构原理。第二个技巧是，几位播客嘉宾提到过，当你遇到难题并找到解决方法后，可以反问它：“我本可以做得不同吗？我本可以说些什么来避免一开始就出错呢？”

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah, that's right. That's right. Yeah, look, on that first one, and again, this is what I'm doing with my 10-year-old. Yeah, look, if you ask me, yeah, this is a really good point. So if you ask an AI, "Write me this code," and then it does it and it comes back and it doesn't work right, if all you know is single function, I asked it and it gave me back something that's not good, what do you even do with that? You don't understand why it gave you that result. Do you even understand what to tell it to try to get it to do something different? (01:00:39): But to your point, if you actually watch what it's doing and then you have the grounding, kind of that leg of your E or your F, if you have that grounding, then you can be like, "Oh, I see what it's doing. I see where it made the mistake. I see where it went sideways." And then you're all of a sudden able to intervene and be able to say, "No, no, that's not what I meant. Do this other thing." And again, this is a big part of having the actual kind of synergistic relationship is that you understand. (01:01:06): And by the way, look, I mean, like everything I'm saying is... everything that we're saying right now also is the same as if you're working with human beings. If you and I are colleagues and I would ask you to do something, you'd come back with something completely different, I do need to understand what was happening in your head in order to be able to give you feedback. If I just tell you, "Oh, that's wrong," nothing happens. I need to actually understand. I need to have theory of mind. I need to understand what you were thinking in order to really give you the right feedback. And again, the great thing with AI is AI will happily sit there and explain all day long why it's doing what it's doing. It'll happily critique itself. (01:01:45): By the way, this is a very fun thing where you can have one AI critique the other AI which is another thing which is you have one AI write the code, you have another AI debunk the code. And so you can actually, you can play the AIs off against each other and get them to argue with each other. And yeah, these are all the kinds of skills that are going to become, I think, incredibly valuable.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。是的，看，就第一个技巧而言，这正是我和我10岁孩子一起做的。是的，如果你问我，这确实是个很棒的观点。所以如果你让AI写一段代码，它完成后却无法正常运行，如果你只懂单一函数，而它给出的代码又不理想，那该怎么办呢？你根本不明白它为什么会这样做。你甚至不知道该怎么告诉它，让它尝试不同的做法？（01:00:39）：但说回你的观点，如果你真正观察它的行为，然后掌握了基础知识——无论是E还是F的知识——有了这样的基础，你就能意识到，“哦，我明白它在做什么。我知道它哪里出错了。我知道它为什么偏离了轨道。”然后你就能立刻介入，说：“不，不，不是你理解的那样。这样做吧。”再说一次，建立这种协同关系的关键在于理解对方。（01:01:06）：顺便说一句，我想我说的所有观点——我们现在讨论的所有内容——都适用于与人类合作的情境。比如，如果你和我是同事，我让你做某件事，而你给出的结果完全不同，我需要了解你当时的思路才能给你反馈。如果我只是说：“哦，你做错了。”那没有任何意义。我需要真正理解。我需要具备心理理论。我需要理解你的想法，才能给你正确的反馈。再说一次，AI的妙处在于，它会乐意整天解释自己的行为。它会乐意自我批评。（01:01:45）：顺便说一句，这是一个非常有趣的场景，你可以让一个AI批评另一个AI——比如让一个AI写代码，让另一个AI去质疑这个代码。这样你就能让两个AI相互较量，让它们互相争论。是的，我认为这些技能将变得极其重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think people call those LLM councils-
turns.zh: 我想人们把这些称为LLM委员会——

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... where they're talking to each other.
turns.zh: ...它们在互相交流。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah, that's right. That's right.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I do feel like if I were... I have no design background. I've always wanted to design. I've always wanted to be a great designer. It feels like that's the hardest one to learn of all these three by just watching and talking because there's a lot of exposure hours as folks have used this term, just like how do you learn to be a great designer. That feels like that's going to be really hard and valuable.
turns.zh: 我确实觉得，如果我……我没有设计背景。但我一直想从事设计工作，一直想成为一名优秀的设计师。相比之下，要想仅通过观察和交流就掌握这门技能，似乎是三者中最难的。正如人们常说的，要想成为优秀的设计师，需要投入大量时间精力。这感觉既困难又宝贵。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: So my true confession is I've always kind of wanted to be a cartoonist, but I have no art skills. But as we're talking, I'm like, "Hmm, it might be time."
turns.zh: 说实话，我一直想成为一名漫画家，但我没有美术功底。不过聊着聊着，我突然觉得：“嗯，或许是时候行动了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The time has come, Marc.
turns.zh: 马克，是时候了。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to pivot to founders, maybe your bread and butter. You spend a lot of time with the most cutting edge, AI-forward founders. I'm curious what you see them do, how you see them, some way they operate that's maybe blowing your mind about how the future of starting a company looks, how the future of AI-forward companies look.
turns.zh: 我想转向创业者这个话题——或许这是你的专长。你与最前沿、最拥抱AI的创业者共处了大量时间。我很好奇，你观察到他们做了哪些事，他们的哪些运营方式令你惊叹？关于创办公司的未来，关于AI驱动型公司的未来，他们又展现了哪些令人惊叹的可能性？

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah. So this is a great and very topical topic that's all playing out in real time right now on the leading edge. So I think there's like three layers of it and see if this makes sense. I think there's like three layers of it. I think layer one is they're thinking, "All right, how does AI redefine the products themselves?" And this is kind of the time-honored kind of thing that happens with technology transitions, and this is kind of what a lot of venture capital is based on which is, okay, there's a new technology that comes out. Maybe it's the personal computer or the iPhone or the internet or now it's AI, and it's like, all right, is this a new capability that gets added to existing products. (01:03:35): So all of a sudden you've got, I don't know, an existing software business and now you've got your PC version of it and now you got your iPhone version of it and you just keep on going and the new technology kind of gets added into the mix with another ingredient to an existing formula, and of course, a lot of new technologies are like that. I don't know when flash storage came out or something, it didn't really redefine the software industry because people just went from using hard disk using flash storage or something. But when the internet came out, like basically old school on-prem software for the most part, not entirely, but a lot of it died and it just got replaced by web software. And so sometimes you get the kind of, it's additive to an existing thing. (01:04:19): Sometimes you get the actually it redefines an entire product category, redefines an industry. In many cases, the companies themselves turn over it. So there's sort of this question, and an example you just mentioned, Nano Banana. So a great example is there are these businesses, like just take Adobe. Photoshop is built a, whatever, 40-year franchise in image editing. Okay, is AI a sort of a feature now that gets added to Photoshop to be able to do AI-based image editing, or do you just stop editing images entirely because you're using Nano Banana and all images are just being generated and it's just easier to just have AI generate a new image than it is to try to edit an old one? (01:04:57): And so I think there's many areas of tech in which that question is being asked and the answers I think will vary by domain. But obviously as a venture firm, we're betting hard on many of these categories being totally reinvented, and a lot of the best founders are trying to figure out how to do that. So that's kind of AI changing the definition of the product. (01:05:16): I think the next layer is actually a lot of what we've already talked about which is AI changing the jobs. And so it's a lot of what we already talked about, but, okay, if I'm a founder of a company and if I have room in my budget for 100 coders, how do I get those coders to be super-empowered AI coders, not the kind of coders I used to have, and if they're super-empowered AI coders, then does that mean, do I still need the 100? Maybe now I only need 10. Or does that mean I still want 100 but now they're doing 10 times more? And so, as you know, a lot of the best founders are working on that right now. (01:05:48): And then I think the third shoe to drop hasn't quite dropped yet, but it's kind of the big one which is, all right, the basic idea of having a company, does that change. And again, here you've got this concept of the super-powered individual which is, okay, can you have entire companies where you have basically the founder does everything. Because what the founder's doing is overseeing an army of AI bots. There's kind of this holy grail in our industry that's been running for a long time which is can you have the one-person billion-dollar outcome. (01:06:21): We've had a few of those over the years. Bitcoin is probably the most spectacular example with Ethereum right behind it which wasn't quite one person but a very small team. You had Instagram and WhatsApp that had very big outcomes with very small teams. Every once in a while you get one of these things where you just, something hits, and you just have a very small number of people associated with it. But that said, most software companies obviously end up with huge numbers of employees. (01:06:46): And so I think the most leading-edge founders are thinking of, okay, how do I reconstitute the actual very definition or idea of having a company and can you have a company that's literally basically just all AI. If you're doing anything in the real world, that's hard, but if you're doing software, that seems like it might be feasible in some cases. (01:07:08): And then there's the ultimate example of that which is can you have like autonomous AI economy stuff happening where you have AI bots on the blockchain or something that are basically out there functioning as a business and making money and just literally where the AI does all the work itself and just issues me dividends. Maybe that's the final outlier result. We have a few founders who are chasing that kind of thing. So I would describe that as kind of the latter that the best founders are on.
turns.zh:
是的。所以这是一个非常热门且极具现实意义的话题，目前正处于前沿领域的实时演进阶段。我认为它可以分为三个层面，看看这样说是否能让大家更清楚。首先，第一层是各家公司在思考：“好吧，AI如何重新定义产品本身？”这正是技术变革中常见的现象，也是很多风险投资的基础逻辑——新技术问世后，比如个人电脑、iPhone、互联网，现在又轮到AI，人们会问：能否将AI功能添加到现有产品中？（01:03:35）举个例子，比如某个现有软件公司，开发了PC版和iPhone版，不断迭代新技术。这类情况下，新技术就像是现有配方中的新成分。当然，许多新技术都是如此。比如闪存存储技术的出现，并未彻底重塑软件行业，因为人们只是从硬盘切换到闪存。但互联网的兴起，基本上终结了传统本地化软件（并非全部，但大部分被淘汰），取而代之的是基于网络的软件。所以有时新技术是现有事物的叠加，有时则彻底重塑整个产品类别或行业，甚至导致公司更迭。（01:04:19）回到具体案例，比如Nano Banana。这类例子表明，许多公司正面临选择：是将AI作为Photoshop的功能模块，还是彻底放弃传统图像编辑，转而使用Nano Banana生成图像？（01:05:16）第二层是我们已讨论过的AI重塑工作岗位。即如何让100名程序员成为超级AI开发者，而非传统开发者。如果成功，是否只需10名程序员？还是现有100名程序员能创造10倍的价值？许多优秀的创业者正为此努力。（01:05:48）第三个尚未完全显现的关键问题是：公司运营模式是否会彻底变革？即是否能由创始人全权掌控整个公司，仅靠AI完成大部分工作。（01:06:03）总之，AI正在重新定义产品、工作岗位和公司模式。（01:06:13）
关于人工智能机器人。我们这个行业长期以来一直追寻着一个圣杯般的目标——能否实现由单人创立就价值数十亿美元的公司。（01:06:21）：过去几年间，我们确实见证过几个这样的案例。比特币无疑是最引人注目的例子，紧随其后的是以太坊，后者虽然不完全是单人创立，但也仅由一个很小的团队完成。Instagram和WhatsApp同样是团队规模很小却能创造巨大价值的典范。偶尔会出现这样的现象——某个创意一鸣惊人，相关团队规模极小。但说实话，大多数软件公司最终都会雇佣大量员工。（01:06:46）：因此，我认为最前沿的创始人正在思考：如何重构公司的定义和理念？能否打造一个完全由人工智能驱动的公司？如果是在现实世界中运作，这显然很难，但在软件领域，某些情况下这或许可行。（01:07:08）：最极致的例子或许是构建自主运行的AI经济体系——让区块链上的AI机器人自主运作、创造收益，所有工作都由AI完成，创始人只需收取分红。或许这才是最终的突破。我们有几位创始人正在追寻这样的目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super interesting. This whole idea of a one-person billion-dollar company, I think it depends on your definition of what this is, like an outcome I could see. Running my newsletter as one person with some contractors, there's so many little annoying things that I have to deal with, with just support tickets and issues and bugs. It's hard for me to imagine actually a one-person billion-dollar company, even if AI is handling so much of your support because there's just so many random-edge cases that I'm just... like filling out forms. And so I guess depends on, do you have contractors, does that count, what does it mean to be a one person. But I'm just like, "I can't see that happening."
turns.zh: 太有意思了。这种一人创立亿级市值公司的概念，我觉得这取决于你如何定义它。比如说，我能想象到这样的结果——运营我的新闻通讯时，虽然有一些承包商协助，但处理用户支持请求、解决问题和修复漏洞的琐碎事务实在太多了。即便让AI来处理大部分支持工作，我也很难想象真能有单人创立亿级市值公司的案例，毕竟总会有各种意想不到的边缘情况，比如填写表格之类的。所以关键在于，你是否有承包商协助？这算不算单人运营？但我就是觉得这很难实现。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, look, Bitcoin, Satoshi pulled it off.
turns.zh: 是啊。我是说，看看比特币，Satoshi就做到了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But the open source community now, does that count? I don't know.
turns.zh: 但现在的开源社区算吗？我不确定。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I guess it counts. Okay.
turns.zh: 我觉得也算吧。好吧。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Right? So yeah, I would say I don't propose to have answers here, but more just like the smartest people I know or many of the smartest people I know are thinking hard about this.
turns.zh: 对呀，就是这样。对吧？所以我不会在这里给出答案，但我认识的很多最聪明的人都在深入思考这个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. What do you think about moats? A big question constantly in AI, the fact that everything's changing, just what's your guys' thesis on moats in AI? Is that even a thing? Do you care?
turns.zh: 是啊。你对护城河怎么看？这是AI领域一直热议的大问题，面对万变的环境，你们对AI领域的护城河有什么见解？这到底是个概念吗？你们关心吗？

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: My experience with really big technological transformations, and of course, I kind of lived this directly with the internet and I saw this happen, is the really big technological transformations, they take a long time to play out and there's all of these structural implications that just kind of cascade out over time. There's this rush to judgment upfront where people say, "Oh, it's therefore obvious that X, Y, Z. It's therefore obvious that this kind of company is going to be the company of the future, not that kind. It's obvious that this incumbent's going to be able to adapt and this other one isn't. It's obvious that there's economic opportunity in this kind of startup and not in these others. It's obvious that the moats are going to be in this area of the technology, but not in this other area." (01:09:25): What everybody does is they kind of state those things with just an enormous amount of self-assurance where they really sound like they have all the answers. And then what happens is these ideas kind of saturate the media because the media naturally prizes definitive answers over open questions because it... it's like when CNBC is booking guests, they want a guest who's going to come on and say, "Yes, this is the way, it's going to be X." Not like, "You know, I think that's a really good question and let's debate it from eight different angles." (01:09:51): What I found is if you look back on those predictions a few years later, and you can do this by the way, if you pull up coverage of the internet from 1993 through 1997, or for that matter even through 2005 or 2010, and you look at the kinds of confidence statements people were making in the first 10 or 15 years, I would say almost all of them were wrong, generally quite badly wrong. And so I think the process, I think there's going to be a massive amount of technological change. It's going to be like, I don't know, five or six layers of structural change that will play out over time. (01:10:26): And again, we've talked about a lot of this, but the implications on what are the definition of products, what are the definitions of companies, what are the definitions of jobs, what are the definitions of industries. How does this play out at the national level? How does this play out at the global level? By the way, how does this intersect with politics? How does this intersect with unions? How does this intersect with war? What's China going to do? And so there are just a tremendous number of unknowns, a very, very large number of unknowns, and I think it's just like really, really dangerous to prejudge these things. (01:11:02): I'll just run this as a thought experiment and you can see what you think on this, but it's like, are AI models themselves defensible. Is there a moat on AI models? And on the one hand, you'd be like, "Wow, it certainly seems like there is or should be," because if something takes billions of dollars to build and you need this incredible critical mass of computing data and there's only a certain number of engineers in the world that know how to do this and they are getting paid like MBA stars. And then these companies have to deal with all these crazy political issues and press issues and reputational stuff and regulatory and legal. (01:11:40): All of that translates to, okay, probably at the end of this, there's going to be two or three companies that are going to end up with like 100%, I don't know, whatever, 50/50 or 30/30/30 or 90/10 and one, or whatever it is, market share and then they're going to have whatever profitability they have and it's going to be kind of a classic oligopoly, or maybe one company's going to win definitively and it'll be a monopoly. And by the way, those outcomes have happened in software many times before. And so maybe that will be the outcome. (01:12:05): The other side of it is if you had told me three years ago that in the Christmas of ChatGPT that within basically a year to year and a half there would be five other American companies that would have basically exactly capable products, and then there would be another five companies out of China that would have exactly capable products, and then there would additionally be open source that was basically the same, I would have been like, "Wow, the thing that seemed like it was black magic all of a sudden has become like commoditized really fast," which by the way, is exactly what happened. Within a year of GPT3 coming out, there were there open source GPT3s running on a fraction of the hardware that were available for free. And then there were five. Now you've got, fully in the game, you've got Google and you've got Anthropic and you've got xAI and you've got Meta and you've got all these other companies that are... and then DeepSeek and Kimi and all these other Chinese companies. And so even at the level of LLMs or AI models, you can squint and make that argument either way. (01:13:05): By the way, same thing at the level of apps. It's like one school of thought is apps are not a thing because the model's just going to do everything, but another way of looking at it is no, actually adapting the model is kind of the engine into a domain involving human beings where you need to actually have it fit for purpose to be able to function in the medical industry or the legal industry or whatever or coding. No, you actually need the application level's actually going to matter enormously, and maybe the LLMs commoditize and maybe the value goes to the apps. And again, you can kind of squint either way on that one, and I know very smart people who are on both sides of that argument. (01:13:41): And so my honest answer on this is I think we're in a process of discovery over time. The way I think about this kind of structurally is it's a complex adaptive system. The technology itself provides one of the inputs. The legal and regulatory process is another input. Actual individual choices made by entrepreneurs matter a lot. The economics matter a lot. Availability of investor capital varies over time, that matters a lot. This is a complex system, and so we actually don't know the outcomes on this yet. We need to be open to surprises at the structural level of what happens. (01:14:19): And of course, as a VC, this is very exciting because it means we're doing this now. We should make bets along every one of these strategies and see how this plays out. I would just say, there may be, I don't know, there may be like one particularly brilliant, I don't know, hedge fund manager or something who has this all figured out, but I guess I would say if they exist I haven't met them yet.
turns.zh:
我的经验告诉我，真正重大的技术变革通常需要很长时间才能显现其影响，期间会产生一系列深远的结构性影响。人们往往急于下结论，轻易得出诸如"因此X、Y、Z显然如此"之类的判断，坚称某类公司必将成为未来领军企业，而另一类则注定失败；声称某家现有巨头能成功转型，而另一家则必将失败；断言某种创业模式蕴含经济机遇，而另一种则徒劳无功；宣称技术壁垒将存在于某个领域而非其他领域。（01:09:25）  
人们常以十足的自信陈述这些观点，听起来仿佛掌握了所有答案。然而这些观点往往被媒体广泛传播，因为媒体天然偏爱确定性答案而非开放性问题，正如CNBC邀请嘉宾时更青睐能断然宣称"是的，技术路径就是X"的嘉宾，而非从多个角度探讨问题的专家。（01:09:51）  
回顾几年前的预测会发现（你完全可以通过查阅1993至1997年间，或2005至2010年间的互联网报道来验证），人们在前十到十五年里做出的许多预测最终都被证明大错特错。未来必将迎来大规模技术变革，这将是分阶段展开的结构性变革，历经五到六层演变。（01:10:26）  
我们已多次探讨过这些变革对产品定义、公司形态、就业类型、行业边界的影响。这些变革将如何在国家层面和全球层面展开？它们又将如何与政治、工会、战争产生交集？中国将如何应对？当前存在着无数未知数，数量之多令人震惊。对此妄下断论实在危险至极。（01:11:02）  
以人工智能模型为例，本身是否具备护城河？一方面，你会认为答案是肯定的，因为构建模型需耗费数十亿美元，依赖海量数据，且全球懂行工程师屈指可数，薪资堪比MBA精英。然而这些公司还要应对疯狂的政治压力、舆论攻击、声誉危机及监管法律困境。（01:11:40）  
最终，市场份额可能集中于两三家巨头，形成100/50/30/90的格局，利润率各异。
接下来可能会形成一种经典的寡头垄断局面，或者某家公司最终会独占鳌头并形成垄断。顺便说一句，软件行业此前就曾多次出现过这样的结局。所以也许这次也会是这样的结果。（01:12:05）：另一方面，三年前如果有人告诉我，在ChatGPT问世的圣诞节前后，基本上在一到一年半的时间内，就会有五家美国公司推出功能几乎完全相同的产品，随后又会有五家中国公司推出类似产品，再加上开源版本也基本一样，我肯定会惊呼：“哇，原本看似神秘的技术突然就变得商品化了！” 而事实也确实如此。GPT3推出一年内，基于开源代码的GPT3模型就能在极低硬件配置下免费运行。如今，谷歌、Anthropic、xAI、Meta等公司，以及DeepSeek、Kimi等中国公司都已全面加入这场竞争。因此，即便在大语言模型（LLM）或人工智能模型层面，人们也可以从不同角度解读这一局面。（01:13:05）：同样，在应用层面也存在类似争议。一派认为应用程序已无存在必要，因为模型能完成所有任务；另一派则认为不然，模型需要针对特定领域进行优化才能适用于医疗、法律或编程等场景。两派观点各有道理，我认识许多对此持不同看法的聪明人。（01:13:41）：所以我的坦率回答是，我们正处于一个逐步探索的阶段。从结构角度看，这是一个复杂的自适应系统。技术本身是输入之一，法律法规是另一输入，创业者的决策至关重要，经济因素同样重要，投资资金的可得性也会随时间波动。这是一个复杂的系统，目前我们尚不确定最终结果。需要对未来可能出现的结构性惊喜保持开放态度。（01:14:19）：当然，作为风险投资人，看到这一切令人兴奋不已，这意味着我们正处在一个充满机遇的时代。我们应该在上述每个战略方向上布局，观察其演变。我想，或许会有某位极具智慧的对冲基金经理或其他人士能看透全局，但至少目前我还没遇到过这样的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing here is don't over-obsess with moats at this point because we have no idea what'll end up being, and as much as it may feel like, okay, there's no way OpenAI will lose this lead, clearly we're seeing a lot of competition. GPT wrapper point is really great. It was such a derogatory term, I don't know, a year ago, just like, "You're just a GPT wrapper." Now it's like the companies that are the biggest companies, the fastest growing companies in the world.
turns.zh: 听起来你的意思是，目前我们不必过度纠结于技术壁垒，因为谁也无法预知最终的局面。尽管人们可能觉得OpenAI的领先优势无可动摇，但我们明明看到市场竞争激烈。GPT封装技术这个概念之前被贬低得不行，就在一年前人们还说“你不过是个GPT封装工具”。如今它却成了全球规模最大、增长最快的科技公司的标配。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah. Well, it's like a little bit like, I don't know, I mean, even just like with... this has been the holiday, three years ago was the holiday of ChatGPT. This last month or whatever has been the holiday of Claude, particularly Claude Code for coding. But it's pretty amazing because it's like, okay, there was Claude which is obviously a great accomplishment, but then there's Claude Code which is an app. It's a Claude wrapper. It's agent harness. And then they did this amazing thing where they came out with, was it Coworker?
turns.zh: 是啊。这有点像，嗯，我是说，就拿……三年前的ChatGPT热潮来说，还有上个月Claude Code在编程领域掀起的风潮。最惊人的是，Claude Code不仅是技术突破，还开发了应用——这就是Claude的封装产品，类似于代理框架。他们还推出了Coworker这个产品，真是令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cowork.
turns.zh: Cowork。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Cowork. And remember what they said of Cowork, which is Claude Code worked Cowork in a week.
turns.zh: Cowork。记得他们怎么说的吗？Claude Code在一周内就完成了Cowork的封装。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, a week and a half, yep, 100%.
turns.zh: 对，一周半，百分之百没错。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Well, and there's two ways looking at that which is like, "Wow, that's really..." I mean, obviously that's really impressive that Claude Code was able to build Cowork in a week and a half. That's great. That's amazing. The other way to look at it is Cowork was developed in a week and a half. How much complexity could there be? How much of a barrier to entry can there be in something that was developed in a week and a half? And then again, it's this push and this pull thing where it's like, wow, it's incredibly functional, incredibly valuable, and people all over the world and every day now are like, "Wow, I can't believe what I can do with this. It's like the most magical product ever." But at the same time, it took a week and a half. (01:16:16): And so every other model company, I'm sure, you'd have to expect, is sitting there being like, "Okay, obviously we need to build an Asian artist and then obviously we need to build a Cowork thing for regular people." I'm not even saying I know anything, but just obviously they're all going to do that. And so how defensible is that? In six months, and we've seen this happen before, is Claude Code going to get lapped the same way that GitHub Copilot got lapped? The history in the last three years has been everything that looks like it's like the fundamental breakthrough gets basically replicated and lapped very quickly. Many of the smartest people I know in the field, when I really talk to them, kind of get a couple drinks into them, they're like, "Yeah." (01:16:55): One theory is there really aren't any secrets among the big labs. The big labs kind of all have the same information and they kind of have all the same knowledge and they lap each other on a regular basis, but there's not a lot of proprietary anything at this point. And then again, evidence of that is DeepSeek came out of left field and basically was like a re-implementation of a lot of the ideas under American big labs and had some original ideas of its own. But, wow, it wasn't that hard for some basically a hedge fund in China to do it, and so how much defensibility is there. (01:17:26): But on the other side of it, you've got, wow, these big labs are now paying individual engineers like they're rock stars and they're incredibly bright and creative people. Maybe there's a dozen nascent ideas at any one of these labs that is actually going to be a huge breakthrough that's going to be hard to replicate. And so again, it's just like, I think we just need... I don't know, my view is I need to put a big discount on my forecasting ability on this one. (01:17:49): For me, it's much less interesting to try to say, "Okay, as a consequence, industry structure in five years is going to be X, the big winner and the category is going to be company Y, the big product killer app is going to be Z." It's like, I don't think I can predict that. I think a much better use of my time is being very flexible and adaptable at a time like this.
turns.zh: 嗯，关于这件事有两种看法。一种是，哇，这真的太了不起了……显然，Claude Code能在一周半内开发出Cowork，这确实令人惊叹。这很棒，太不可思议了。另一种看法是，Cowork是在一周半内开发出来的。那它能有多复杂呢？对于一周半就能开发出来的产品，进入门槛能有多高呢？再说了，这就像是一种推拉效应。一方面，它功能强大、价值非凡，全球各地的人们每天都在惊叹：“哇，真不敢相信我能用它做这么多事。这简直是最神奇的产品了。” 但另一方面，它只用了一周半时间开发出来。（01:16:16）：我敢肯定，其他模型公司肯定都在想：“好吧，我们显然需要开发一个针对亚洲艺术家的产品，然后再开发一个面向普通用户的Cowork产品。” 我不是说我知道什么内幕，但显然他们都会这么做。那么这能有多具防御性呢？六个月后，正如我们过去见证的那样，Claude Code会不会像GitHub Copilot那样被超越？过去三年的历史表明，任何看似根本性突破的产品，都会迅速被复制和超越。我认识的业内最聪明的一些人，当我和他们聊天，喝上几杯酒后，他们都会说：“是啊。” （01:16:55）：有一种理论认为，顶尖实验室之间其实没有什么秘密。这些实验室基本掌握着相同的信息和知识，经常互相模仿，但目前没有什么专有技术。另一个证据是DeepSeek的横空出世，它基本上就是对美国大型实验室许多理念的重新实现，还加入了自己的创新点。但令人惊讶的是，中国的一家对冲基金就能做到这一点，所以防御性到底有多强？（01:17:26）：但另一方面，顶尖实验室现在给个别工程师的报酬就像给摇滚明星一样，他们都是极其聪明和有创造力的人。也许这些实验室中任何一个都有十几个初步想法，最终会成为难以复制的重大突破。所以再次强调，我认为我们只需要……我不知道，我的观点是，我需要大大降低对此的预测能力。 （01:17:49）：对我来说，试图说“好吧，因此五年后的行业结构将是X，大赢家将是Y公司，大杀手级应用将是Z”，这样做没多大意思。我觉得我预测不了。我认为在这种时候，最好保持灵活和适应能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So with all this in mind, do you feel like there's something you're paying attention to more to help you decide, okay, this is where we want to place our bet, or is the answer essentially the strategy you guys have, which is place a lot of bets? You guys raised the largest fund in history. Is that the way you win in this world?
turns.zh: 所以综合以上种种，你们觉得有没有什么需要更关注的方面来帮助你们做出决定，比如，好，就是这个地方我们要下注，还是说答案基本上就是你们采用的策略，即下很多注？你们筹集了史上最大规模的基金。这就是你们在这个世界里获胜的方式吗？

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, for us, yeah. For us, we obviously have a very deliberate strategy. One way to think about this the Peter Thiel... You remember the Peter Thiel formulation of... he said, "There's a two by two, there's optimism and pessimism, and then there's determinant and, is it indeterminate, and indeterminate." And so he always argued that Silicon Valley is characterized by too much what he calls indeterminate optimism. What he meant by that is basically, I think the way he would describe it is an indeterminate optimist who thinks the world is going to be better but can't explain why. Some combination of things is going to happen to make the world be better even if we don't know what those things are. I think he at least historically would say that's basically... that risks at least being just wishful thinking or delusional thinking. (01:19:11): What the world needs more is determinant optimists, which are people who are like, "No, the world is going to be better because I'm going to do this specific thing." He would classify, for example, Elon, he would sort of maybe say VCs are indeterminate optimists and then he would say Elon is the determinant optimist where it's like, no, I'm going to build the electric car, I'm going to do solar, and then I'm going to do Mars and these very concrete things. (01:19:35): I think there's a lot to Peter's framework, but the way I would describe it is I think maybe if he and I disagree with part of that it would be I think the indeterminate optimism is a stronger phenomenon than at least I think he's historically represented it as, and I would put myself firmly in the indeterminate optimist category, and that's the strategy that we have at a16z which is... and the reason for that is hopefully it's not so much wishful thinking. It's more, no, the indeterminate optimism of venture capital or the indeterminate optimism of a16z or Silicon Valley is actually very specific which is there are these extremely bright and capable people, like Elon and many others, who are founders and kind of product creators. Each of those individual people is a determinant optimist. Each of them individually has a very strong view of what they're going to do, but the great virtue of the capitalist system, the great virtue of the American economy, the great virtue of Silicon Valley is we don't just have one of those and we don't just have 10 of those. We have 100 and a thousand and then 10,000 of those. (01:20:34): The way to optimize the outcome is to have as many of those as possible be as good as possible, run as hard as possible. And then just the nature of the future is like we just don't know all the answers and that's okay. And then the right way to deal with that is to run as many experiments as possible and have as many smart people try to do as many interesting things as possible. And so, yeah, I would put myself firmly on the side of the indeterminate optimistic.
turns.zh:
是的。我的意思是，对我们来说，是的。对我们而言，我们显然有非常明确的战略。谈到这个问题，彼得·泰尔（Peter Thiel）曾提出一个观点……你还记得彼得·泰尔的论点吗？他说：“存在一个二维坐标系，分别是乐观主义和悲观主义，以及确定性与不确定性。”他一直认为硅谷的特点是过多的“不确定性乐观主义”。他的意思是，基本上，我认为他会把这种不确定性乐观主义描述为一种模糊的乐观主义——即认为世界会变得更好，但却无法解释其中的原因。尽管我们不知道具体会发生什么，但某些因素的组合会让世界变得更好。至少在历史上，泰尔会说这基本上……这种不确定性乐观主义可能只是一种一厢情愿的想法或幻想。

（01:19:11）：世界更需要的是确定性乐观主义者，即那些会说：“不，世界会变得更好，因为我要做这件具体的事。”的人。例如，他会把埃隆（Elon）归类为确定性乐观主义者，而风险投资家可能被他视为不确定性乐观主义者。埃隆则会说：“不，我要造电动汽车，我要做太阳能项目，然后我要探索火星”——这些都是非常具体的行动。

（01:19:35）：我认为泰尔的框架有很多可取之处，但我的理解是，如果我和他在某些观点上存在分歧，那可能是因为泰尔所描述的不确定性乐观主义比历史上呈现的更为极端。我会把自己坚定地归入不确定性乐观主义者的行列。这也是我们a16z所遵循的战略——之所以如此，并非仅仅是一厢情愿的想法。相反，风险投资的不确定性乐观主义或硅谷的不确定性乐观主义实际上非常具体，即有许多极其聪明和有能力的人，比如埃隆和其他许多创始人及产品创造者。这些个体都是确定性乐观主义者。他们每个人都对自己要做的事情有非常坚定的看法，但资本主义制度、美国经济和硅谷的伟大之处在于，我们不只有一个这样的人，也不只有10个这样的人。我们有100个、1000个，甚至10000个这样的人。

（01:20:34）：优化结果的方法是让尽可能多的人尽可能优秀，尽可能努力地工作。未来的本质就是我们并不知道所有的答案，但这没关系。正确的应对之道是尽可能多地进行实验，让尽可能多的聪明人尝试做尽可能多有趣的事情。所以，是的，我会坚定地站在不确定性乐观主义者的阵营里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm wondering if the answer to the question of what you look for now more and more is this determinant optimistic founder that has this massive ambition and is-
turns.zh: 我在想，现在你越来越多地寻找的对象是否是这种确定性乐观主义的创始人，他们拥有宏大的抱负，并且——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... [inaudible 01:21:00] Optimistic founder-
turns.zh: ……[01:21:00未听清]乐观主义的创始人——

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... and has this massive ambition and is actually working on achieving it.
turns.zh: ……并且拥有宏大的抱负，并且实际上正在努力实现它。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. No, that's right, that's right. I mean look, the founders need to be determinate optimists. They need to have a very specific plan. And look, the critique always... The critique from the founders is, "Oh UVCs have it easy, because you don't actually have to commit, right? You don't actually have to, like, make... You have to make the bed you lay in, you can, like, place multiple bets you can have. Whereas a portfolio, you should have a lot more sympathy for us as founders, because we only get to make the one bet." (01:21:31): And there's truth to that. The kind of argument on that is the founders get to run their companies, we don't. So, we don't get to put our hand on the steering wheel. And so, the great virtue of being a determinant optimist is you actually get to single-mindedly execute against that goal. (01:21:48): And look, in the long run, who does history remember? History remembers Henry Ford, right, not whoever was, whatever the seed investor who seeded Ford Motor Company, and 10 other car companies have failed. Right? (01:21:58): And so, the determinant optimist is the founder of the company builder and the engineer, and these are the people who actually use the sign, and deserve 99.9999% of the credit. But you know, having said that, I do think there is a role for having some indeterminate optimists in the background, no, helping along the way, and helping keep the whole cycle going.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。不，没错，没错。我是说，看吧，创始人需要是坚定乐观主义者。他们需要有一个非常明确的计划。还有，批评者总是说……批评者会说，“哦，风险投资公司（UVCs）日子好过，因为你们实际上不需要下定决心，对吧？你们不需要真的去……人总是要为自己铺好路，你们可以下多个赌注。而对投资组合公司来说，大家应该更体谅我们创始人，因为我们只能下这一次赌注。”（01:21:31）：这话不无道理。这种争论的核心在于，创始人可以运营自己的公司，而我们不行。所以，我们无法掌控方向盘。坚定乐观主义者的优点在于，你可以一心一意地朝着目标前进。（01:21:48）：还有，从长远来看，历史会铭记谁？历史记住的是亨利·福特，对吧？而不是种子投资者投资福特汽车公司的人，以及其他10家失败的汽车公司。是吧？（01:21:58）：所以，坚定乐观主义者是公司创始人，是工程师，这些人才是真正执行的人，值得99.9999%的功劳。不过话说回来，我确实认为背后有一些不那么坚定乐观的人也有其作用，不，帮助推动整个循环。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you think about AGI in shifting your investment thesis? Like, as we approach AGI and hit AGI, as an investor, how do you think about your investment thesis changing?
turns.zh: 你在考虑AGI（通用人工智能）时会调整你的投资论点吗？比如，当我们接近AGI并迎来AGI时代，作为投资者，你认为你的投资论点会如何变化？

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah, so I've always kind of had a little bit of an issue... I've always kind of struggled with the concept of AGI because at least... Well, let's put it this way. Let's define terms which is where I kind of struggle with it. Which is, there's like the prosaic definition of AGI, and then there's like the cosmic definition. (01:22:48): And the way I describe it as, so let me start with the cosmic one. So the cosmic one is basically, is the singularity, right? And so, AGI is the moment where you enter the singularity which is to say where the world fundamentally changes. And the rules of the old world are gone, we're now operating in a new domain. (01:23:04): And then the full definition of singularity is it's a world in which human judgment is no longer really relevant because you get this self-improvement loop, the AI is improving itself. In a sort of race circle takeoff scenarios, you could see if this takeoff thing, where the AI's improving itself, and the machines are making decisions so much faster than people, and people are just sitting there watching the machine do its thing. (01:23:26): And I kind of described it, I don't really think we live in that world, whether they could call that utopian or dystopian, I don't think we're lucky or unlucky enough to live in that world. We could debate that, we could talk about that more. (01:23:37): But the prosaic definition of AGI that at least I think the industry purchases but it's kind of conversed on, and tell me if you agree with this, is when the AI could do every economically-relevant task as good as a person.
turns.zh: 是啊，所以我一直有点纠结……我一直有点纠结于AGI这个概念，因为至少……嗯，换个说法。先定义术语，这就是我纠结的地方。也就是说，AGI有平凡的定义，也有宏大的定义。（01:22:48）：我这样描述一下，先从宏大的定义说起。宏大的定义基本上就是奇点，对吧？所以AGI就是你进入奇点的时刻，也就是说世界从根本上发生变化。旧世界的规则消失了，我们现在在一个新领域中运作。（01:23:04）：然后奇点的完整定义是，这是一个人类判断不再真正相关的世界，因为AI会自我改进。在某种赛博朋克式的起飞场景中，你可以看到这种起飞情况，即AI自我改进，机器比人类做决策快得多，而人类只是坐在那里看着机器做事。（01:23:26）：我这样描述的，我不认为我们生活在那个世界里，不管人们称之为乌托邦还是反乌托邦，我不认为我们足够幸运或不幸运地生活在那个世界里。我们可以对此进行辩论，可以多聊聊。（01:23:37）：但AGI的平凡定义，至少我认为行业接受但也有争议的，是当AI能够像人类一样做好每一项经济相关的任务时。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The way the co-founder of Anthropic put it is, like, "A basket of the most valuable economic tasks," so it's, like, 10, 15, not every single economically-valuable task.
turns.zh: Anthropic的联合创始人是这样说的：“一篮子最有价值的经济任务”，所以是10个、15个，不是每一项经济有价值的任务。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Okay, got it. Yeah, so it's maybe even a slightly reduced definition. And by the way, we're clearly getting close to that if we're not already there. (01:24:04): And so on that one, I kind of feel like, so I kind of feel like the cosmic one overstates what's going to happen. And then I kind of feel like the kind of AGI definition that you just gave, I think it kind of understates what's going to happen. It's almost too reductionist. (01:24:17): And the reason for that is, I don't think there's any reason to assume that human skill level is the cap on anything. Right? And so the way we say that is AGI always is the definition you gave, the definition I gave. It's always kind of relative in comparison to a human worker, right? (01:24:33): And it's, like, I don't know, human skill level caps out at a certain point, but that's because of the inherent biological limitations of the human organism. Right? Human, I gave you an example. Human IQ, kind of what they call "fluid intelligence," or the sort of G factor of fluid intelligence, IQ I think tops out in humans as a species, it tops out around 160. (01:24:56): Right? Where at like 160 it's like Einstein level, Einstein [inaudible 01:25:00]-
turns.zh: 好的，我明白了。是啊，所以这或许甚至是一个稍微简化的定义。顺便说一句，如果我们还没有达到那个阶段，那我们显然也快了。（01:24:04）：关于这个问题，我觉得所谓的宇宙级定义夸大了未来可能发生的情况。而你刚刚给出的通用人工智能（AGI）定义，又让我觉得它低估了现实。这种定义几乎太过简化了。（01:24:17）：原因在于，我认为没有理由假设人类的技能水平是任何事物的上限，对吧？所以我们常说AGI总是按照你给出的定义，或者我给出的定义来定义。它总是相对于人类工人来衡量的，对吧？（01:24:33）：我不知道，人类的技能水平在某个点上会达到极限，但那是因为人类生物体固有的生理限制。对吧？我给你举个例子。人类智商，也就是所谓的“流体智力”，或者流体智力的G因素，我认为人类作为一个物种的智商最高值在160左右。（01:24:56）：对吧？160左右的智商水平，就相当于爱因斯坦的智商水平，爱因斯坦[01:25:00不可听清]——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In terms of IQ. Yeah.
turns.zh: 就智商而言。是的。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: ... in terms of IQ. Like, it just tops out at 160. The 160 IQ people are the ones who come up with new physics, there's only a small handful of those. Generally speaking, when we run into somebody in the world who's like incredibly smart, who's like a bestselling author, or like a, you know, one of the world's best, I don't know, research scientists, or one of the world's best doctors, whatever it would be, probably 140 is kind of the IQ that you're looking for there. (01:25:26): If you're looking for a really good lawyer, it's probably 130. If you're looking for a really good line manager in a business, it's probably 110. If you're looking for an accountant, like a small business accountant, who's good at doing the books for small businesses, it's probably 105. Right? (01:25:41): And so the kind of scope of impressive human... The ability of the human organism to do intellectually impressive things, it's sort of that 110 to 160 is kind of the spectrum, and good news is there's a lot of those people running around, but there's not that many at 140, 150, 160. (01:25:57): But it's like, that's like the limitations of what can fit in here, right? And it's like, there's no theoretical limit on where this goes if you release the limitations of human biology, right? And so, can you have a... And you already have people running these experiments to kind of do human-equivalent kind of IQ for existing AI models. (01:26:17): And by the way, existing AI models are kind of testing around the 130, 140 level, which means they're going to get to the 160 level. And they're arguably on the math side starting to get to the 160 level now. (01:26:26): But I think we're going to have AI models relatively quickly that are going to be like 160, 180, 200, 250, 300. By the way, and I think that's great, right? I feel as great about that as I do about the fact that we occasionally get an Einstein. Right? (01:26:41): It's like, would the world be better off or worse off with more or fewer Einsteins? And the answer is, of course the world would be better off with more Einsteins, and of course the world would be better off with machines that have more IQ like Einstein or greater than Einstein. (01:26:51): But I think IQ of the machines is going to exceed that of the humans, I think that's really good. And then the performance, again, it goes back to like the AI coding thing that's happening. Performance against task is going to get better also. (01:27:02): I think this is where Linus Torvalds in particular was like, "Yeah, okay, this thing is starting to generate better code than I can." Okay? So now we're going to have AI coders that are actually better coders than the best human coders. I think that's... Right? (01:27:13): I think we're going to have AI doctors that are better than the best human doctors, I think we're going to have AI lawyers that are better than the best human lawyers, which actually is going to be very interesting to see, which we can talk about. Which I think is also great. (01:27:24): And so, I don't think there's a... I think we're used to living in a world where we just don't understand how good good can get, because we've been capped by our own biology. And we're going to get to experience what it's like when you have the capability at your fingertips, that's actually better than human in these domains. (01:27:38): So you see what I'm saying, which is, like, I think this idea of human equivalent is just going to be a footnote. It's like, "Oh yeah, that was just on Tuesday, in 2026 is when they hit that." And it kind of didn't matter because the next question was, like, "Okay, what do we get to do in a world where we actually have machines that are better than that?" Right? (01:27:58): And so, I think this is going to be much more of an exploratory process for actually seeding human capability than it's going to be any sort of particular singular singularity moment or whatever that happens, that just happens to coincide with the human threshold.
turns.zh:
就智商而言。比如，智商最多能达到160。那些智商高达160的人，是能够开创新物理学理论的科学家，但这类人凤毛麟角。一般来说，当我们遇到极其聪明的人，比如畅销书作家，或者世界顶尖的研究科学家、医生之类的，他们的智商大概在140左右。（01:25:26）如果你在找优秀的律师，智商可能要130 分；如果是企业中的优秀管理者，智商可能要110 分；如果是小型企业的会计师，擅长处理账务的，智商可能要105 分。对吧？（01:25:41）所以，人类令人惊叹的智力能力范围大概在110到160之间。好消息是，这样的人其实很多，但140、150、160分的人就比较少了。（01:25:57）但这就是人类智力极限的范围，对吧？如果不受人类生物学的限制，理论上智商能达到多高呢？所以，你已经有研究团队在尝试让现有的人工智能模型达到人类智商水平。（01:26:17）顺便说一下，现有的人工智能模型智商测试结果大约在130到140之间，这意味着它们最终会达到160分。而在数学方面，它们现在已经开始接近160分了。（01:26:26）但我认为很快就会有智商达到160、180、200、250、300的AI模型。顺便说一句，我觉得这很棒，对吧？就像我们偶尔能遇到爱因斯坦一样，我对此同样感到欣喜。对吧？（01:26:41）那么，世界上如果多些或少些爱因斯坦，是更好还是更糟呢？答案当然是，多些爱因斯坦对世界更有益，拥有超过爱因斯坦智商的机器对世界同样有益。（01:26:51）但我认为机器的智商会超过人类，这真的很棒。然后是性能问题，回到正在进行的人工智能编程领域。面对特定任务的性能也会不断提升。（01:27:02）我觉得这正是Linus Torvalds所说的：“是的，好吧，这个东西开始生成比我更好的代码了。” 对吧？所以现在我们将有比最优秀的人类程序员更出色的AI程序员。我觉得这真的……对吧？（01:27:13）我认为我们将有比最优秀的人类医生更出色的AI医生，比最优秀的人类律师更出色的AI律师，这真的很值得期待，我们可以继续讨论。我觉得这也很棒。（01:27:24）所以，我不认为存在……我们习惯生活在一个无法理解人类极限的世界里，因为我们被自身生物学所限制。但我们即将亲身经历当你手中掌握的能力在某些领域实际上比人类更强时的情景。（01:27:38）所以你明白我的意思了，就是，我认为“人类等同”这个概念只会成为历史注脚。人们会说：“哦，对了，那是在2026年的周二，他们达到了这个水平。” 但这其实并不重要。
接下来那个问题是：“好吧，在一个我们真的拥有比人类更强大的机器的世界里，我们能做些什么呢？” 对吧？（01:27:58）所以，我认为这将更多地是一个探索性的过程，旨在真正激发人类的潜能，而不是某个特定的奇点时刻之类的，而这种探索恰好与人类的技术门槛相契合。

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Well, I don't know if you have this experience, I have this experience all the time. Well, two experiences I have all the time. Whatever, I want to have this theory on this thing, or to have a plan or whatever. (01:28:39): And it's just like, "Fuck," I don't have the eight hours, or by the way, the eight weeks or the eight years, right? And I just don't know enough yet, and I'm just, like, I can't do the math in my head, and my memory isn't perfect, and I can't remember, and I read... I don't know if you have this, you get interested in something, you read 10 books. And then you're like, "Shit, I forgot almost everything I just read." (01:29:01): I wish I could retain it all but I can't. It's just like you just have this... I sort of live in this state of endless frustration. And so it's like, if I could just be smarter than I was, I'd be much better at what I do, but I'm not. So there's that. (01:29:14): And I don't know how often you have this, but I have this on a regular basis. It's just like, "I," because of what we do, I know a bunch of people who I know for fucking sure are smarter than I am. And I know it because when I talk to them, I just find myself at a certain point. It's like for the first half of the conversation, I'm just taking notes the entire time. And for the second half of the conversation, I'm just like, "Fuck," like, "Fuck me." Like, this person is just smarter than I am, and they're just out-thinking me, and they're going to keep out-thinking me, and I just can't, and I'm just like, "All right, goddammit. I've got to go home and I've got to have a drink." (01:29:43): Because I'm just not... Whatever that is, I'm not that. And so, we're just so used to having those limitations, that the idea of having machines that work for us that don't have those limitations, I just... I think that's much more exciting than people are giving it credit for.
turns.zh: 嗯，我不知道你是否有过这种经历，我自己一直深有体会。嗯，我有两个一直存在的困境。第一个是，我知道自己应该能做到某件事，但就是做不到……花费的时间太长了，我想写点东西，或者想……管他呢，想研究某个理论、制定个计划之类的。（01:28:39）结果就只能说：“妈的，八小时根本不够，更别提八周或八年了。” 对吧？而且我还不够精通，脑子里算不过账，记忆力也不完美，读了书也记不住。不知道你有没有过这种经历，对某个东西感兴趣后，读了十本书，结果发现几乎把刚读的内容都忘了。（01:29:01）真希望能全记住，但做不到。这种挫败感简直无处不在。所以要是我能比现在更聪明些，做事就会顺利得多，但现实并非如此。所以就只能接受现实了。（01:29:14）不知道你多久会遇到这种情况，但我经常碰到。比如因为我们的工作，认识很多比我聪明得多的人。通过交谈就能明显感觉到，前半段我一直在疯狂记笔记，后半段就只能说：“妈的，真是服了你。”这种人就是比我聪明太多，他们思维超前，而且会一直领先下去，我却无能为力，只能说：“好吧，该死的，我得回家喝一杯了。” 因为我就是……总之，我达不到那种水平。所以我们习惯了这些局限，想到有台机器能替我们思考却没有这些限制，我就……我觉得这比人们想象的要激动人心得多。

turns.en: Oh man. I could talk to you for hours, Mark. I'm thinking to close out the conversation, I want to ask about your media diet and your product diet. I saw an interview with you where you're just like, "Airpods changed my life, I'm just listening to audiobooks now all the time." turns.zh: 天哪，马克，我能跟你聊上好几个小时。我想结束这次对话前，问问你的媒体消费习惯和产品使用习惯。你刚提到书，读了十本，我记得你总是在读书。看过你采访，说“AirPods改变了我的生活，现在我总是在听有声书。”（01:30:17）那说到媒体消费，你最近在读什么、关注什么，比如播客、新闻简报、博客之类的，还有特别喜欢的书吗？

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. So what I read is basically, I mean I read... So I read basically three categories of things. So in terms of general media, it's basically I sort of... I always describe it as I have an almost perfect barbell strategy, which is I read X, and I read old books. Right? (01:30:41): So it's basically either, like, up-to-the minute what's happening right now, or it's like a book that was written 50 years ago that has stood the test of time, and then where presumably there's something timeless in it. And then it's sort of everything in the middle, I'm always much more skeptical about. (01:30:56): And in particular, it's kind of what I already said, which is I think if you go back and you read old... Nobody ever does this, it's actually really funny, there's no market for it. But if you go back and you read old newspapers... And by the way, you can do this, just read the last week's newspaper, right? Yeah, today, so we're taping on Friday. So read last Friday's newspaper, right? (01:31:15): And just go back and read it, and be like, "Oh my God. None of this happened. None of what they predicted played out the way that they said that it would. None of this turned out to actually be that relevant or correct." They didn't understand, by the way, they had no view of what was going to happen this week. Then they couldn't know, and so they were making predictions and forecasts and so forth based on not having information. (01:31:37): But it's like, "Wow, none of this happened, I wish I had never read this, oh my God." And then it's kind of the same thing with magazines, I go back and read old magazines, and just the level of just the endless numbers of predictions that they make. And kind of, you know, the problem with... Newspapers at least they're going day-to-day, the thing with magazines is it's like a week or month kind of a long cycle. (01:31:58): And so by the time an article even hits publication, it's often out of date. So I just have a big problem with kind of everything in the middle. And so it's either of the moment or timeless. But then yeah, you mentioned newsletters. I mean, so the other thing, and this is maybe obvious, but I think it's probably still underrated, which is actual practitioners in the field who are actually creating content, I think probably is still dramatically underrated. (01:32:21): And I think this is a huge part of the Substack phenomenon, and the newsletter phenomenon, and the podcast phenomenon, is, like, direct exposure to the people who are actually principals in the field who actually know what they're talking about is probably still dramatically underrated. (01:32:33): And I think again, the reason for that is like we're used to being in this mass media kind of culture in which basically everything is mediated. Right? Everything got filtered through like TV interviews or, like, newspaper interviews, or magazine interviews. And obviously now more and more it's just, no, you actually want smart people who are actually working on something explaining themselves. (01:32:49): And then you have tons of intermediation, like podcasts, that kind of open that up for people and make that possible. And so yeah, domain practitioners are really great. I mean, yeah, just to state the obvious in AI, it's obviously your stuff, but also, like, the fact that Lex Fridman can have the world's leading... And any of you guys, there's a small handful of you guys who have access to these people, you could have the world's leading experts in the domain actually show up. (01:33:15): And by the way, and look, the critique always is, people talk their book, like if I'm running a startup or whatever I'm just selling. But it's like... And there's always a little bit of that... But it's also, my experience is people love to talk about what they do. And they fundamentally want to express what they do, and they want to explain it, and they want people to understand it. (01:33:35): And everybody kind of enjoys that, and they get to contribute to human knowledge by doing that, and they get ego gratification by doing that. And so I think there's actually just tremendous amounts of alpha in listening to the world's leading experts in the space who actually just show up and talk about what they're doing. (01:33:48): And of course the world is awash in that today in a way that it wasn't as recently as 10 years ago. So yeah, I do as much of that as I can too.
turns.zh:
是啊，是啊。所以我读到的大概是，我是说我读到的……我读的基本上可以分为三类内容。就一般媒体而言，基本上我会……我常说自己有一种近乎完美的杠铃策略，就是我读X，然后读旧书。对吧？（01:30:41）：所以基本上要么是关于当前时事的最新动态，要么是50年前写的经受住了时间考验的书籍，而这些书里大概都有永恒的价值。然后就是介于两者之间的内容，我对这些总是持怀疑态度。（01:30:56）：特别是，我之前说过，如果你回头去读旧报纸……没人这么做，其实挺有趣的，市场对这类内容不感兴趣。但如果你回头去读旧报纸……顺便说一句，你现在就可以这么做，就读上周的报纸，对吧？（01:31:15）：然后回头去读，心里会感叹：“天哪，这些根本没发生。他们预测的结果和实际情况完全不符。这些内容根本不相关，也不准确。”顺便说一句，他们根本不了解本周会发生什么。他们当时不可能知道，所以他们在没有信息的情况下进行预测和预判。（01:31:37）：但你会惊讶地发现，这些预测全都落空了。真希望自己从未读过这些内容，天哪。” 然后杂志的情况也类似，我回头去读旧杂志，里面有无数的预测。问题在于……报纸至少是日更的，而杂志是以周或月为周期的。（01:31:58）：所以一篇文章发表时，往往已经过时了。所以我对介于两者之间的内容都持怀疑态度。要么是即时的，要么是永恒的。但你提到了新闻通讯。我是说，还有一点可能显而易见，但我认为仍被低估的，那就是实际从业者在领域内创造内容的人，他们可能仍被严重低估。（01:32:21）：Substack现象、新闻通讯现象和播客现象的核心在于，直接接触真正在该领域工作的、真正懂行的人。这可能仍被严重低估。（01:32:33）：我认为原因在于，我们习惯了大众媒体文化，所有内容都经过过滤。比如电视采访、报纸采访、杂志采访。现在越来越多的是，你希望真正聪明、正在做事的人来解释自己。（01:32:49）：然后还有大量的中介，比如播客，为人们打开了这样的可能。所以是的，领域从业者真的很棒。以AI为例，显然你的内容很棒，但比如，Lex Fridman能接触到世界顶尖的……你们当中有少数人能接触到这些人，让领域内的顶尖专家亲自现身。（01:33:15）：顺便说一句，看看这些内容……
批评总是存在的，人们总爱夸夸其谈。比如说，我经营一家初创公司时，别人就会问我创业经历。但这种情况其实挺常见的……以我经验来看，人总爱谈论自己做的事。他们从根本上想展示自己的成果，解释自己的思路，让别人理解自己的工作。（01:33:35）大家都乐在其中，通过这种交流为人类知识库添砖加瓦，还能满足自我满足感。所以我认为，多听听行业领军人物讲述他们的工作心得，实在是获益匪浅。（01:33:48）当然，如今全世界充斥着这样的内容，这比十年前要普遍得多。所以我也尽可能多地参与这种交流。

turns.en: And there's also just this culture in tech, Silicon Valley, in particular, of sharing, or not trying to keep these secrets. Everyone on LinkedIn is always like, "How is this free?" Like, it's just the way it works.

(01:35:44): It's just, right, the indeterminate optimism of ecosystem flexibility of the ecosystem that they Silicon Valley could morph into all these categories, and again, maybe a testimony to indeterminate optimism.

turns.speaker: Marc Andreessen
turns.en: Have you not heard of it? Okay, so you're going to really enjoy it. So, I won't spoil too much of it, so at the surface level the following spoils nothing. So at the surface level, it's set in a small town in New Mexico called Eddington which is a small town about 600 people. (01:37:04): And there's a sheriff who's played by Joaquin Phoenix who's like an old, crusty, basically right-winger, and then there's a mayor played by Pedro Pascal who's basically a young, hip, progressive. And then the movie starts I think in March of 2020. (01:37:21): And so it starts when COVID first hits. And then it sort of as it plays out over the next few months, it intersects, and it sort of extends into the summer of 2020. So, kind of the George Floyd moment and then protests and riots and kind of everything. (01:37:36): So sort of the convergence of COVID and then all the BLM stuff. And then there's a third kind of element to it which is there's a company which is basically a loosely-disguised version of Meta if you read the backstory of it, which is building an AI data center on the outskirts of town. So they kind of pull that in as sort of a thing that looms larger and larger over time. (01:37:58): And then the thing it really is great at is it really shows, you know, this is a small town in New Mexico. And so, everybody in the town gets full wrapped up in all the COVID stuff, and they get fully wrapped up in all the BLM stuff, and they get fully wrapped up in all the tech anxiety stuff. (01:38:13): But they're all experiencing it basically through the internet, right? Which is what actually happened, right? So the reason I love the movie so much is one is it's the first movie that directly grapples with 2020, of what happened in 2020, and it just, like, fully, fully engages and grapples with all the dynamics that were playing out in the country. (01:38:31): But the other reason is it's the first movie that does a really good job of showing what it was like especially in that area to live in a world in which there were things happening in the real world, and people were kind of experiencing events online, like in a way that was very central in their lives. Right? (01:38:45): And so it does a really good job of pulling in smartphones and social media in a way that movies really, really, really struggle with, and then the whole thing comes together in an incredibly entertaining way. (01:38:55): And so I wouldn't even say I completely agree with the movie or whatever, and I think the director of the movie and I would probably disagree about a lot, but he really tries hard to really grapple with what it's actually like to live like a human being in the 2020s in America in a way that I think many other filmmakers who are very talented have just been very scared of touching. (01:39:14): And this guy, for some reason he's just like, "Yeah, I'm just going find all the third rails and I'm just going to fucking grab them."
turns.zh: 你没听说过？好吧，你肯定会喜欢的。我先不剧透太多，从表面上讲不会剧透太多。故事背景设定在新墨西哥州一个叫埃丁顿的小镇，人口只有600左右。（01:37:04）影片从2020年3月新冠疫情刚爆发时讲起，然后随着时间推移，穿越整个2020年，经历了乔治·弗洛伊德事件、抗议暴乱等种种社会变革。（01:37:21）还有第三个元素，片中有个公司，仔细一看就是隐晦影射Meta的，他们在小镇边缘建AI数据中心，逐渐成为压倒骆驼的最后一根稻草。（01:37:58）影片最棒的地方在于，它真实呈现了新墨西哥州小镇的生活。所有居民都深陷新冠疫情、BLM运动和科技焦虑的漩涡，却又都通过网络获得信息。这不正是2020年的真实写照吗？我爱这部片子的原因，一是它首部直面2020年的乱象，完整还原了美国社会的撕裂。二是它突破了传统电影叙事，将现实与网络世界交织成令人信服的叙事结构。（01:38:31）更难得的是，它以极具代入感的方式呈现了小镇居民在真实世界遭遇变故，却又在网络世界寻找慰藉的困境。（01:38:45）导演用巧妙手法处理了智能手机与社交媒体的呈现方式，这在电影中实属不易，最终以极具娱乐性的方式将所有元素融合在一起。（01:39:14）虽然我不完全认同片中观点，但导演确实努力捕捉了2020年代美国人的生存状态，这是许多才华横溢的导演避之不及的主题。
